title: AI as an Assistive Tool — Module Quiz

items.q: What distinguishes an access gain from a convenience gain?
options: Access gains save more time
Access makes something possible that was not possible for that person
Access gains only apply to registered disabilities
items.explain: Convenience makes an easy thing faster and you could still do it yourself. Access changes whether it can be done independently at all.

items.q: Why does assistive use demand higher reliability than ordinary use?
options: Assistive tools are used more often
You may be unable to check the output, so an undetectable error is worse than no answer
The underlying models are less accurate
items.explain: E7's verification advice assumes you could read, see or hear the original. "I could not check" is different from "I checked".

items.q: This module positions AI relative to established assistive technology as:
options: A replacement for screen readers and AAC devices
A useful addition, especially where a task previously needed another person
Unnecessary for anyone with existing tools
items.explain: Established assistive technology is mature and specialised. AI does not need to be more than an addition to that toolkit.

items.q: For an official letter you must act on, you usually want:
options: A much shorter summary
A reshaping that keeps every fact but changes the presentation
A translation into more formal English
items.explain: A summary leaves things out. When a document has consequences, you want everything kept and presented differently.

items.q: The most important line to add to any simplification request:
options: Keep it under 200 words
List every condition, exception or 'only if' from the original
Use a friendly tone
items.explain: "Eligible if resident six months and not claiming elsewhere" becoming "You can get a reduction" is shorter, clearer and wrong.

items.q: Before reaching for AI to make text readable, you should first:
options: Change size, spacing, line length, contrast and typeface
Convert the document to plain text
Ask someone else to read it
items.explain: Those five are free, instant and frequently sufficient. Reshaping with AI is for documents you cannot restyle.

items.q: Why does 'dictate, then tidy' work when writing is difficult?
options: Dictation is faster than typing
It separates having the thought from producing correct text
Spoken language is simpler than written
items.explain: If your difficulty is the second part, splitting them removes the barrier without handing over what you wanted to say.

items.q: Does using dictation and tidying change who authored the work?
options: Yes — any AI involvement transfers authorship
No — the test is whether you can defend every choice, and the thinking stayed yours
Only for work that will be assessed
items.explain: It is no different in kind from a spellchecker or a scribe. The line is the argument itself, not the typing.

items.q: Instead of 'describe this image', a blind user should usually ask:
options: For a longer, more detailed description
The specific question they actually need answered
For the description in bullet points
items.explain: Specific questions get shorter, more accurate answers, and a non-answer to a specific question is obvious in a way a paragraph is not.

items.q: The most valuable instruction when using a camera to read something:
options: Be concise
If you cannot tell, say so — do not guess
Describe the colours precisely
items.explain: Without it you get a plausible answer to everything. With it you learn the photo is too blurred and can retake it.

items.q: Which should never rest on an image description alone?
options: Identifying a tablet or its dose
Working out what a poster advertises
Checking whether a photo is in focus
items.explain: Medication, signatures, money and safety all need a second route — a pharmacist, an official accessible copy, or a person.

items.q: Automatic captions fail most on:
options: Long sentences
Names, jargon, crosstalk, accents and poor audio
Fast speech alone
items.explain: Several of those are properties of the room rather than the software, which is where the leverage is.

items.q: The single most effective way to improve caption accuracy:
options: A more advanced captioning service
One person speaking at a time, close to a decent microphone
Asking everyone to speak slowly
items.explain: A cheap headset outperforms any amount of processing, and half a second between speakers removes most crosstalk errors.

items.q: What do automatic captions systematically fail to convey?
options: The words themselves
Tone, silence and interruption
The order in which people spoke
items.explain: Whether that was a joke, and whether silence meant agreement, are exactly what human captioners and interpreters convey.

items.q: When a task will not start, the obstacle is usually:
options: The amount of work involved
That the first step is undefined, and defining it needs the capacity that is missing
Insufficient motivation
items.explain: "Sort out the insurance" is a category, not a task. Finding the five-minute action inside it is the hard part.

items.q: Why forbid a plan when asking for a first step?
options: Plans take longer to produce
A twelve-item plan is a new thing to feel behind on — you asked for a door, not a map
Plans are usually wrong
items.explain: The request is for the single smallest startable action, and a list undoes the point of asking.

items.q: The condition attached to relying on external memory:
options: It must be digital
Capture has to be reliable, or your head keeps holding everything anyway
It must be reviewed every day
items.explain: If things only sometimes get written down, you maintain two systems and trust neither.

items.q: When asking what a message meant, you should request:
options: The single most likely interpretation
Two or three possible readings
A drafted reply
items.explain: A single confident interpretation sounds authoritative and is a guess. You are learning how words commonly land, not what someone meant.

items.q: Rehearsing a difficult conversation works better if you ask the assistant to:
options: Be encouraging so you gain confidence
Be more resistant than you think is likely
Summarise rather than act it out
items.explain: Practising against an easy version teaches you nothing. The point is finding where your argument falls apart.

items.q: Why not adopt a polished draft of a difficult message wholesale?
options: It may contain factual errors
It sets an expectation of a register you then have to sustain in person
It is usually too long
items.explain: The reply comes back pitched to someone who writes like that — in a conversation you already found difficult.

items.q: Good alt text describes:
options: Everything visible in the image
What the image is doing in this particular context
The file name and dimensions
items.explain: The same photograph needs different alt text on a flood article than on a page about that car model.

items.q: For a decorative image beside text that already says everything:
options: Write a full generated description
Use an empty alt attribute so screen readers skip it
Leave the alt attribute off entirely
items.explain: Filling every alt with description makes pages noisier rather than more accessible, and omitting the attribute is not the same as an empty one.

items.q: Publishing uncorrected automatic captions is:
options: Acceptable, since some captioning is better than none
Generally not adequate provision, and can be worse than nothing
Required before a video can be published
items.explain: They look like provision while conveying something else. Names and technical terms have to be fixed before publication.

items.q: When someone tells you what they need in order to take part:
options: Assess whether the request is reasonable
Ask what would help and do it — the request is the end of the enquiry
Ask an assistant how best to accommodate them
items.explain: People have usually spent years refining what works, and their disability is their information to share rather than yours to process.
